docs.title: Photovoltaic Cell Model
docs.text:
The single-diode PV cell model:

\[I = I_{ph} - I_0\left(e^{\frac{q(V + IR_s)}{nk_B T}} - 1\right) - \frac{V + IR_s}{R_{sh}}\]

Where: - Iph: Photocurrent (proportional to irradiance) - I0: Diode reverse saturation current - q: Elementary charge (1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C) - n: Ideality factor (1-2) - kB: Boltzmann constant (1.38×10⁻²³ J/K) - T: Junction temperature (K) - Rs: Series resistance (Ω) - Rsh: Shunt resistance (Ω)

Simplified form (ignoring Rs and Rsh): $\(I = I_{ph} - I_0 e^{qV/(nk_B T)}\)$

docs.title: Maximum Power Point (MPP)
docs.text:
Power output: P = V × I

At the MPP, the voltage-power curve has zero slope: $\(\frac{dP}{dV} = 0 \implies I + V\frac{dI}{dV} = 0\)$

Key characteristics: - MPP voltage ≈ 0.7–0.8 × Voc (open-circuit voltage) - Varies with temperature and irradiance - Typical PV module: Vmpp ≈ 30V (at STC: 1000 W/m², 25°C) - Array: Series/parallel connection to reach desired voltage

docs.title: Temperature Dependence
docs.text:
MPP voltage decreases with temperature: $\(V_{mpp}(T) = V_{mpp,ref} - \alpha(T - T_{ref})\)$

Where α ≈ 0.5 mV/°C (temperature coefficient, negative).

docs.title: Perturb and Observe (P&O)
docs.text:
Simplest and most common algorithm:

Loop at time interval Ts:
  1. Measure V(k), I(k), P(k) = V(k) × I(k)
  2. Calculate ΔP = P(k) - P(k-1), ΔV = V(k) - V(k-1)
  3. Update reference:
     if ΔP > 0
       if ΔV > 0
         V_ref = V_ref + ΔV_step  (moved right on curve)
       else
         V_ref = V_ref - ΔV_step  (moved left on curve)
     else
       if ΔV > 0
         V_ref = V_ref - ΔV_step  (moved away from MPP)
       else
         V_ref = V_ref + ΔV_step  (moved away from MPP)

Advantages: Simple, few computations Disadvantages: Oscillates around MPP (can be reduced with small step size)

docs.title: Incremental Conductance (IncCond)
docs.text:
More sophisticated, detects MPP directly:

\[\frac{dI}{dV} = -\frac{I}{V} \quad \text{at MPP}\] 
Loop at time interval Ts:
  1. Measure ΔI/ΔV (conductance change)
  2. Calculate I/V (instantaneous conductance)
  3. Compare:
     if ΔI/ΔV = -I/V       → At MPP, hold V_ref
     if ΔI/ΔV > -I/V       → Left of MPP, increase V_ref
     if ΔI/ΔV < -I/V       → Right of MPP, decrease V_ref

Advantages: Fast tracking, no steady-state oscillation Disadvantages: More computation, noise sensitivity

docs.title: Grid Synchronization via PLL
docs.text:
The Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) detects the phase angle of the grid voltage:

                    ┌───────────────┐
vgrid ──────────────┤  Normalize &  │
                    │  Filter (LP)  │
                    └────────┬──────┘
                             │ sin(θ_grid)
                             ▼
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │  Multiplier   │ × V_ref
                    │   (demod)     │
                    └────────┬──────┘
                             │ e_pll
                             ▼
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │  PI Control   │
                    │               │
                    └────────┬──────┘
                             │ ω_pll
                             ▼
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │  Integrator   │
                    │  θ_pll = ∫ω   │
                    └───────────────┘
                             │
                             └──► θ_grid estimate

PLL Equations:

Error signal: e_pll = vgrid × sin(θ_pll - θ_grid) ≈ Vgrid·(θ_pll - θ_grid)

Angular frequency: ω_pll = ω_grid + Kp·epll + Ki·∫epll

Tuning: Bandwidth ≈ 50-100 Hz (fast PLL locks to grid variations)

docs.title: Current Control for Grid Injection
docs.text:
Reference Current Generation:

The inverter injects current in phase with grid voltage: $\(i_{ref} = I_{max} \sin(\omega_e t + \theta_pll)\)$

Where Imax is set by available PV power: $\(I_{max} = \frac{P_{pv}}{V_{grid,rms}}\)$

Reactive Power (Optional):

For grid support, inject reactive current: $\(i_{ref} = I_d \sin(\omega_e t + \theta_{pll}) + I_q \cos(\omega_e t + \theta_{pll})\)$

Where Id = active current, Iq = reactive current.

Current Control Loop:

         i_ref
           │
      ┌────┴────┐
      │    -    │
      └────┬────┘
           │ i_error
           ▼
      ┌─────────┐
      │   PI    │
      │ Control │
      └────┬────┘
           │ v_ref
           ▼
    ┌─────────────┐
    │    SPWM     │
    │ (carrier)   │
    └─────┬───────┘
          ▼
    ┌─────────────┐
    │  Inverter   │
    │  Switches   │
    └─────────────┘

docs.title: Anti-Islanding Protection
docs.text: Detects when the grid is disconnected (preventing island formation).

docs.title: Passive Detection Methods
docs.text:
1. Frequency Drift: If grid disconnects, frequency drifts (no stiff voltage source)
  2. Voltage Drift: RMS voltage deviates from nominal
  3. Rate of Change: dV/dt or df/dt monitoring

docs.title: Active Detection Methods
docs.text:
1. Frequency Shift (Frequency Bias): Inject small frequency offset; detect via grid coupling
  2. Reactive Power Injection: Inject reactive power and observe voltage response
  3. Voltage Shift: Modulate voltage injection level

docs.text: Parameter Trip Level Trip Time Overvoltage (>150% Vnom) 264V 0.16 s Undervoltage (<85% Vnom) 170V 2 s Overfrequency (>52 Hz) 52 Hz 0.16 s Underfrequency (<48 Hz) 48 Hz 0.16 s

docs.title: Step 1: PV Array Configuration
docs.text: For 200-450V DC input: - Typical module: 40V at MPP - Series: 5-10 modules (200-400V nominal) - Parallel: 2-3 strings (increases current)

docs.title: Step 2: MPPT DC-DC Converter
docs.text:
Design a boost/buck converter: - Input: 200-450V DC (PV array) - Output: 400V DC (regulated) - Power: 5 kW

Equations: $\(D = 1 - \frac{V_{pv}}{V_{out}}\)$ $\(L = \frac{V_{pv}(1-D)}{f_{sw} \Delta I_L}, \quad \Delta I_L = 0.2 \times I_{pv}\)$ $\(C = \frac{I_{pv} D}{f_{sw} V_r}\)$

docs.title: Step 3: Full-Bridge Inverter
docs.text:
Select switches for 400V DC bus: - IGBT or SiC MOSFET rated for 600V minimum - Switching frequency: 16 kHz (balance switching loss vs. filter size) - Deadtime: 200-500 ns

Gate driver PWM frequency: fsw = 16 kHz Modulation index: Ma = 0.9 (for linear region)

docs.title: Step 4: Output L-C Filter
docs.text:
Reduce high-frequency switching ripple: $\(L = \frac{V_{dc}}{8 f_{sw} I_{max}}, \quad C = \frac{I_{max}}{8 f_{sw} V_r}\)$

Example: L = 5 mH (reduces di/dt), C = 5 μF (10% voltage ripple)

docs.title: Step 5: PLL Tuning
docs.text:
For 50 Hz grid, typical PLL bandwidth 50-100 Hz: $\(K_p = 2 \times BW, \quad K_i = BW^2\)$

For BW = 100 Hz: Kp = 200, Ki = 10000

docs.title: Step 6: MPPT Tuning
docs.text: Sampling interval: 100 ms (slow update, stable) Step size: ΔVref = 5V (balance speed vs. oscillation)

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. PV Curve Tracing: Measure I-V and P-V curves at different irradiance levels
  2. MPPT Algorithm: Implement P&O or IncCond, verify tracking efficiency >99%
  3. PLL Synchronization: Measure phase error; tune for fast lock (<100 ms)
  4. Current Injection: Verify sine wave injection in phase with grid (PF > 0.98)
  5. THD Measurement: Measure output voltage THD; design filter for <3%
  6. Anti-Islanding: Simulate grid disconnection; verify detection within 2 seconds
  7. Efficiency Mapping: Plot efficiency vs. load and irradiance
  8. Reactive Power: Inject Q = ±2 kVAr for grid support if applicable

docs.text: Variable-speed wind turbine power conversion system.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Modern wind turbines use variable-speed operation: - Maximum energy capture (MPPT) - Full power conversion (Type 4) - Grid code compliance - Fault ride-through capability

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Generator Type PMSG Rated Power 2 MW Speed Range 8-20 RPM Grid Connection 690V, 50 Hz DC Link 1100V

docs.title: Wind Power
docs.text:
\[P_{wind} = \frac{1}{2}\rho A v^3\]

Where: - ρ = air density (1.225 kg/m³) - A = swept area - v = wind speed

docs.title: Power Coefficient
docs.text:
\[P_{turbine} = C_p(\lambda, \beta) \cdot P_{wind}\]

Maximum Cp ≈ 0.48 (Betz limit = 0.593)

docs.title: Tip Speed Ratio
docs.text:
\[\lambda = \frac{\omega R}{v}\]

Optimal λ ≈ 6-8 for modern turbines

docs.title: Tip Speed Ratio Control
docs.text: Wind Speed ──► λ_opt ──► ω_ref ──► Speed Control ──► Generator

docs.title: Power Curve Control
docs.text:
Generator Speed ──► P_opt Curve ──► Torque Ref ──► Generator
\[P_{opt} = K_{opt} \cdot \omega^3\]

docs.title: Power Control
docs.text: $\(P^* = P_{turbine} - P_{losses}\)$ $\(Q^* = Q_{grid,ref}\)$ (from grid operator)

docs.title: Low Voltage Ride-Through (LVRT)
docs.text: During grid faults: - Inject reactive current for voltage support - Limit active power - Maintain DC link voltage

docs.title: DFIG Alternative
docs.text: Doubly-Fed Induction Generator: - Reduced converter rating (30%) - Partial speed range (±30% of sync) - More complex control - Brush maintenance

docs.title: Analysis Tools
docs.text:
How to measure, analyze, and export simulation results in GeckoCIRCUITS.

Duration: 15 minutes

Prerequisites: Running Simulations

docs.title: The SCOPE (Oscilloscope)
docs.text: The SCOPE block is the primary tool for viewing simulation results.

docs.title: Opening the Scope
docs.text: Double-click any SCOPE block in the schematic to open the waveform viewer.

docs.title: Scope Channels
docs.text:
Each SCOPE input terminal corresponds to a channel. Channels display:

  • Voltage signals from voltage probes
  • Current signals from current probes
  • Control signals from control blocks

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Action How Zoom in Scroll wheel up Zoom out Scroll wheel down Pan Click + drag Auto-scale Right-click > Auto Scale Reset view Right-click > Reset

docs.title: Cursors
docs.text:
Use cursors for precise measurements:

  1. Right-click in the scope > Add Cursor
  2. Drag cursor to the point of interest
  3. Read the time and value display

docs.title: Using Two Cursors
docs.text:
With two cursors, you can measure:

  • Time difference (delta t) between two points
  • Value difference (delta V or delta I)
  • Frequency = 1 / delta t

docs.title: Average and RMS
docs.text:
For periodic signals, the scope can compute:

Measurement Formula Use For Average (1/T) x integral of v(t) dt DC component RMS sqrt((1/T) x integral of v^2 dt) Power calculations Peak max(v(t)) Component stress Peak-to-peak max - min Ripple measurement

docs.title: Ripple
docs.text:
Voltage or current ripple is the AC component on top of the DC:

\[\Delta V = V_{max} - V_{min}\] \[\text{Ripple (\%)} = \frac{\Delta V}{V_{avg}} \times 100\]

docs.title: Efficiency
docs.text:
\[\eta = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} = \frac{V_{out} \times I_{out}}{V_{in} \times I_{in}}\]

Measure input and output power using voltage and current probes.

docs.title: Power Factor
docs.text:
For AC circuits:

\[PF = \frac{P_{real}}{P_{apparent}} = \frac{P}{V_{rms} \times I_{rms}}\]

docs.title: THD (Total Harmonic Distortion)
docs.text:
\[THD = \frac{\sqrt{V_2^2 + V_3^2 + V_4^2 + ...}}{V_1}\]

Use the FFT view in the scope for harmonic analysis.

docs.title: FFT Analysis
docs.text: The scope includes a frequency-domain view using Fast Fourier Transform:

docs.title: Viewing the Spectrum
docs.text:
1. Run simulation to steady state
  2. Open scope
  3. Switch to FFT view (if available)
  4. Observe harmonic content

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text: Feature Indicates Fundamental peak Switching frequency Harmonics Integer multiples of f_sw Low-frequency content Control loop dynamics Broadband noise EMI concerns

docs.title: Export to CSV
docs.text:
From the scope:

  1. Right-click > Export Data
  2. Choose CSV format
  3. Select channels to export
  4. Save file

docs.title: Post-Processing
docs.text:
Exported data can be analyzed in:

  • MATLAB/Octave - data = readmatrix('output.csv');
  • Python - data = numpy.loadtxt('output.csv', delimiter=',')
  • Excel - Open directly as CSV

docs.title: Thermal Measurements
docs.text:
When thermal simulation is enabled:

Measurement Unit Description Junction temperature C Semiconductor die temperature Switching losses W Energy lost during transitions Conduction losses W I^2 x R losses during ON state Total losses W Switching + conduction

See Thermal Simulation Tutorials for details.

docs.title: Tips for Good Analysis
docs.text:
1. Wait for steady state - Don't measure during startup transients
  2. Use enough cycles - Average over multiple switching periods
  3. Check time step - Too large a step hides high-frequency content
  4. Compare with theory - Verify results match analytical predictions
  5. Document settings - Record simulation parameters with results

docs.title: Building Circuits
docs.text:
Learn how to create power electronics circuits from scratch in the GeckoCIRCUITS editor.

Duration: 20 minutes

Prerequisites: First Simulation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Building a circuit involves four steps:

  1. Place components on the schematic
  2. Wire them together
  3. Set parameters for each component
  4. Add measurement points (SCOPE)

docs.title: Step 1: Start a New Circuit
docs.text: Go to File > New (Ctrl+N) to create an empty schematic.

docs.title: Adding Components
docs.text:
1. Select a component from the component palette (left panel or menu)
  2. Click on the schematic to place it
  3. The component appears at the clicked location

docs.title: Component Categories
docs.text:
Power electronics circuits typically need:

Category What to Place Why Sources Voltage source Provides input power Switches MOSFET, IGBT, Diode Switching elements Passive L, C, R Energy storage and filtering Ground Ground symbol Required - voltage reference Control PWM, Constant Switch gate signals Display SCOPE View simulation results

docs.title: Rotating and Flipping
docs.text:
• Right-click a component for rotation options
  • Rotate to align terminals for clean wiring

docs.title: Making Connections
docs.text:
1. Click on a component terminal (small square)
  2. Click to add wire waypoints (corners)
  3. Click the destination terminal to complete the connection

docs.title: Wiring Tips
docs.text:
Clean Schematics

  • Use horizontal and vertical wires only
  • Align components on the grid
  • Keep signal flow left-to-right, top-to-bottom

docs.title: Common Wiring Mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Symptom Fix Missing ground Simulation fails Add ground to return path Open node "Floating node" warning Connect all terminals Shorted source Infinite current Add series resistance/inductance

docs.title: Step 4: Set Parameters
docs.text: Double-click each component to set its values.

docs.title: Example: Buck Converter Parameters
docs.text: Component Parameter Example Value V_source Voltage 48 V MOSFET (default) - Diode (default) - Inductor L 100 uH Capacitor C 47 uF Resistor R 10 Ohm PWM Frequency 100 kHz PWM Duty Cycle 0.25

docs.title: Unit Prefixes
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS recognizes standard SI prefixes:

Prefix Symbol Value mega M 10^6 kilo k 10^3 milli m 10^-3 micro u 10^-6 nano n 10^-9 pico p 10^-12

docs.title: Placing a SCOPE
docs.text:
1. Add a SCOPE block from the control components
  2. Connect signals you want to measure to the scope inputs
  3. Each input becomes a channel in the oscilloscope

docs.title: What to Measure
docs.text:
For a typical power converter, measure:

  • Output voltage across the load
  • Inductor current through the inductor
  • Switch node voltage at the switching point

docs.title: Using Voltage and Current Probes
docs.text:
• Voltage probe - Measures voltage between two nodes
  • Current probe - Measures current through a component (place in series)

docs.title: Example: Build a Buck Converter
docs.text: Follow these steps to build a basic buck converter from scratch:

docs.title: Circuit Topology
docs.text:
Vin ──[MOSFET]──●──[L]──●── Vout
                    │        │
                 [Diode]   [C]  [R]
                    │        │    │
                   GND ──────●────┘

docs.title: Step-by-Step
docs.text:
1. Place Vin - DC voltage source, set to 48V
  2. Place MOSFET - Connect drain to Vin positive
  3. Place Diode - Cathode to MOSFET source, anode to ground
  4. Place Inductor - From switch node to output
  5. Place Capacitor - From output to ground
  6. Place Resistor - From output to ground (load)
  7. Connect Ground - To source negative, diode anode, capacitor, resistor
  8. Add PWM - Connect to MOSFET gate (100 kHz, D=0.25)
  9. Add SCOPE - Connect to output voltage node

docs.title: Verify Before Running
docs.text:
Checklist:

  • All nodes connected (no floating nodes)
  • Ground present
  • Source has a return path
  • Switch has a control signal
  • SCOPE connected to measurement points
  • Simulation time step appropriate (< 0.1 us for 100 kHz)

docs.title: Simulation Settings
docs.text:
Before running, set appropriate simulation parameters:

Parameter Value Why Total time 1 ms ~100 switching periods Time step 50 ns 200 steps per period Solver Backward Euler Stable for switching circuits

docs.title: Your First Simulation
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through opening, running, and analyzing a circuit simulation in GeckoCIRCUITS.

Duration: 15 minutes

Prerequisites: Installation complete

docs.title: Step 1: Launch GeckoCIRCUITS
docs.text:
Start the application using your platform's launcher:

./scripts/run-gecko-linux.sh    # Linux/WSL
./scripts/run-gecko-macos.sh    # macOS
scripts\run-gecko.bat           # Windows

The main window opens with an empty schematic editor.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Example Circuit
docs.text:
Go to File > Open and navigate to:

resources/tutorials/1xx_getting_started/101_first_simulation/ex_1.ipes

This loads a basic power converter circuit. You should see:

  • Power components (top) - Switches, diodes, passive components
  • Control blocks (bottom) - PWM generators, signal sources
  • SCOPE blocks - Oscilloscope measurement points

docs.title: Step 3: Understand the Circuit
docs.text: Before running, take a moment to understand the schematic:

docs.title: Components You'll See
docs.text: Component Symbol Role DC voltage source Circle with ± Provides input power MOSFET switch Triangle with gate Controlled switching element Diode Triangle with bar Freewheeling current path Inductor (L) Coil symbol Stores energy, smooths current Capacitor (C) Parallel plates Filters output voltage Resistor (R) Zigzag Load Ground Three lines Reference node SCOPE Rectangle Measurement display

docs.title: Viewing Component Parameters
docs.text:
Click on any component to see its dialog with parameters like:

  • Resistance, inductance, capacitance values
  • Voltage/current source settings
  • Switch timing and control signals

docs.title: Step 4: Configure Simulation
docs.text:
Open the simulation settings via Simulation > Settings or click the settings icon.

Key parameters:

Parameter Meaning Typical Value Total time (T) How long to simulate 10 ms Time step (dt) Computation interval 1 us Solver Numerical method Backward Euler

Time Step Rule

The time step should be 100x smaller than the switching period. For 100 kHz switching: dt < 0.1 us

docs.title: Step 5: Run the Simulation
docs.text:
Click Run (play button) or press F5.

Watch the progress bar - the simulation computes all circuit variables at each time step.

Typical simulation time: 1-5 seconds for simple circuits.

docs.title: Step 6: View Results
docs.text: Double-click any SCOPE block to open the oscilloscope window.

docs.title: Reading the Oscilloscope
docs.text:
The scope displays voltage and current waveforms over time:

  • X-axis - Time (seconds)
  • Y-axis - Voltage (V) or Current (A)
  • Multiple channels - Different colors for different signals

docs.title: Scope Navigation
docs.text: Action Control Zoom in Scroll wheel up Zoom out Scroll wheel down Pan Click + drag Auto-scale all axes Right-click > Auto Scale Add cursor Right-click > Cursor

docs.title: Step 7: Analyze the Results
docs.text:
For a buck converter, you should observe:

  1. Output voltage - Settles to V_out = D x V_in
  2. Inductor current - Triangular ripple waveform
  3. Switch voltage - Rectangular pulses between V_in and 0

docs.title: What to Check
docs.text:
• Does the output reach steady state?
  • Is the ripple within acceptable limits?
  • Are there any unexpected spikes or oscillations?

docs.title: Step 8: Experiment
docs.text:
Try modifying the circuit:

  1. Change duty cycle - Click the PWM block, adjust D
  2. Change load - Click the resistor, change R
  3. Change inductance - Click the inductor, change L
  4. Re-run and compare results

Undo

Use Edit > Undo (Ctrl+Z) to revert changes.

docs.text: GeckoCIRCUITS runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Follow the instructions for your operating system.

docs.title: Java 21
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS requires Java 21 or later.

WindowsLinux (Ubuntu/Debian)Linux (Fedora/RHEL)macOS
  1. Download Eclipse Temurin JDK 21
  2. Run the installer
  3. Verify installation: 
    java -version

sudo apt update
sudo apt install openjdk-21-jdk
java -version

sudo dnf install java-21-openjdk-devel
java -version

# Using Homebrew
brew install openjdk@21

# Add to PATH
echo 'export PATH="/opt/homebrew/opt/openjdk@21/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

java -version

openjdk version "21.0.x" 2024-xx-xx
OpenJDK Runtime Environment (build 21.0.x+xx)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (build 21.0.x+xx, mixed mode)

  2. Download the latest GeckoCIRCUITS-x.x-<platform>.zip
  3. Extract to your desired location
  4. Run the launcher script

# Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/tinix84/GeckoCIRCUITS.git
cd geckocircuits

# Build with Maven
mvn clean package assembly:single -DskipTests

Maven Installation

WindowsLinuxmacOS

Download from maven.apache.org and add to PATH

sudo apt install maven  # Debian/Ubuntu

docker run -p 8080:8080 gecko-rest-api:latest

docs.title: PWM Basics
docs.text:
Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) is the fundamental control method for power electronics. This tutorial explains how PWM works and how to use it in GeckoCIRCUITS.

Duration: 15 minutes

Prerequisites: Building Circuits

docs.title: What is PWM?
docs.text:
PWM converts a DC input voltage to a controllable output by rapidly switching a transistor on and off.

     ON        OFF       ON        OFF
    ┌───┐            ┌───┐
    │   │            │   │
────┘   └────────────┘   └────────────
    |←D·T→|←(1-D)·T→|

T = switching period = 1/f
D = duty cycle (0 to 1)

docs.title: Key Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Symbol Unit Description Switching frequency f_sw Hz How fast the switch toggles Switching period T = 1/f_sw s Duration of one cycle Duty cycle D - Fraction of period the switch is ON (0-1) ON time t_on = D x T s Time switch conducts OFF time t_off = (1-D) x T s Time switch is off

docs.title: Why PWM?
docs.text:
The average output voltage is proportional to the duty cycle:

\[V_{out,avg} = D \times V_{in}\]

By varying D from 0 to 1, you can control the output from 0V to V_in.

docs.title: The PWM Block
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS provides a built-in PWM control block:

Inputs: - Carrier frequency (f_sw) - Duty cycle (D)

Output: - Digital signal (0 or 1) that drives the switch gate

docs.title: Setting Up PWM
docs.text:
1. Place a PWM block from the control components
  2. Double-click to set parameters:
  3. Frequency: e.g., 100 kHz
  4. Duty Cycle: e.g., 0.5 (50%)
  5. Connect the output to the switch gate terminal

docs.title: PWM Generation Methods
docs.text: Method Description Use Case Fixed duty cycle Constant D value Open-loop testing Comparator-based Compare reference to carrier Closed-loop control Signal-based External signal sets duty cycle MATLAB/Python control

docs.title: Buck Converter
docs.text: \[V_{out} = D \times V_{in}\] D V_in = 48V V_out 0.25 48V 12V 0.50 48V 24V 0.75 48V 36V

docs.title: Frequency Selection
docs.text:
Choosing the right switching frequency involves trade-offs:

Higher Frequency Lower Frequency Smaller L and C needed Larger L and C needed Higher switching losses Lower switching losses Faster transient response Slower transient response More EMI Less EMI

docs.title: Typical Frequencies by Application
docs.text: Application Typical f_sw Motor drives 10-20 kHz DC-DC converters 50-500 kHz LED drivers 100 kHz - 2 MHz RF power 1-100 MHz

docs.title: Exercise: PWM Parameter Sweep
docs.text:
Try this experiment with the buck converter:

  1. Open resources/tutorials/1xx_getting_started/103_pwm_basics/ex_3_pwm.ipes
  2. Run with D = 0.25, observe V_out
  3. Change D to 0.50, re-run, compare
  4. Change D to 0.75, re-run, compare

Expected results:

D Expected V_out 0.25 ~25% of V_in 0.50 ~50% of V_in 0.75 ~75% of V_in

docs.title: Dead Time
docs.text:
In half-bridge and full-bridge circuits, complementary switches must never be ON simultaneously (shoot-through). A dead time is inserted between turn-off and turn-on:

Switch 1: ─────┐           ┌─────
               └───────────┘
                 |← dead →|
Switch 2: ──────┘time     └──────
                ─────────────

GeckoCIRCUITS supports dead-time configuration in the PWM block for bridge topologies.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Get up and running with GeckoCIRCUITS in 5 minutes.

docs.title: 1. Launch the Application
docs.text:
Linux / WSLWindowsmacOS 
./scripts/run-gecko-linux.sh

scripts\run-gecko.bat

./scripts/run-gecko-macos.sh

Or run directly with Java:

java -Xmx3G -Dpolyglot.js.nashorn-compat=true \
  -jar target/gecko-1.0-jar-with-dependencies.jar

docs.title: 2. Open an Example Circuit
docs.text:
Go to File > Open and navigate to:

resources/tutorials/2xx_dcdc_converters/201_buck_converter/buck_simple.ipes

This opens a basic buck converter circuit - one of the most common DC-DC power topologies.

Quick Open

You can also pass a circuit file as a command-line argument: 

java -jar target/gecko-1.0-jar-with-dependencies.jar \
  resources/tutorials/2xx_dcdc_converters/201_buck_converter/buck_simple.ipes

docs.title: 3. Explore the Schematic
docs.text:
The circuit editor shows the buck converter topology:

  • MOSFET switch - controlled by a PWM signal
  • Diode - freewheeling path for inductor current
  • Inductor (L) - energy storage element
  • Capacitor (C) - output voltage filter
  • Resistive load (R) - the load being powered
  • SCOPE - oscilloscope to view waveforms

You can click on any component to see and edit its parameters.

docs.title: 4. Run the Simulation
docs.text:
Click the Run button in the toolbar or press F5.

The simulation will execute for the configured duration. You'll see the progress in the status bar.

docs.title: 5. View Results
docs.text:
Double-click the SCOPE component to open the oscilloscope window. You should see:

  • Output voltage settling to the target value
  • Inductor current with triangular ripple waveform
  • Switch node voltage toggling between input voltage and ground

docs.title: Oscilloscope Controls
docs.text: Action How Zoom in/out Mouse scroll wheel Pan Click and drag Auto-scale Right-click > Auto Scale Measure Right-click > Cursor

docs.title: 6. Modify Parameters
docs.text:
Try changing the duty cycle to see how it affects the output:

  1. Click the PWM component
  2. Change the duty cycle parameter
  3. Re-run the simulation (F5)
  4. Compare the new output voltage

The buck converter relationship is: V_out = D x V_in, where D is the duty cycle (0-1).

docs.text:

  • Component placement and connections
  • Parameter values for each component
  • Scope/measurement configuration
  • Simulation settings (time step, duration)

docs.title: Running Simulations
docs.text:
How to configure and run simulations in GeckoCIRCUITS.

Duration: 10 minutes

Prerequisites: Building Circuits

docs.title: Simulation Settings
docs.text: Access via Simulation > Settings or the toolbar gear icon.

docs.title: Essential Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description How to Choose Total time (T_end) Simulation duration 10-100x switching period Time step (dt) Computation interval < T_sw / 100 Solver Numerical method See solver table below

docs.title: Time Step Selection
docs.text:
The time step is the most critical setting. Too large causes errors; too small wastes computation time.

Rule of thumb: dt < 1/(100 x f_sw)

Switching Freq Max Time Step Recommended 10 kHz 1 us 500 ns 50 kHz 200 ns 100 ns 100 kHz 100 ns 50 ns 500 kHz 20 ns 10 ns

docs.title: Simulation Duration
docs.text:
Choose enough time for the circuit to reach steady state:

  • Fast circuits (> 100 kHz): 0.1 - 1 ms
  • Medium circuits (10-100 kHz): 1 - 10 ms
  • Slow circuits (< 10 kHz, motors): 10 - 100 ms
  • Thermal transients: 1 - 100 s

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS offers three fixed-step solvers:

Solver Accuracy Stability Best For Backward Euler (BE) 1st order Very stable Default choice, stiff circuits Trapezoidal (TRZ) 2nd order Can oscillate Accuracy-critical circuits Gear-Shichman (GS) Multi-step Stable Large circuits

docs.title: Which Solver to Use?
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Start] --> B{Circuit type?}
    B -->|Switching converter| C[Backward Euler]
    B -->|Linear/analog| D[Trapezoidal]
    B -->|Large circuit| E[Gear-Shichman]
    C --> F{Oscillations?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Reduce time step]
    F -->|No| H[Good to go]

Start with Backward Euler

When in doubt, use Backward Euler. It's the most stable and works well for most power electronics circuits. Switch to Trapezoidal only if you need higher accuracy for resonant or filter circuits.

docs.title: Interactive Mode
docs.text:
1. Press F5 or click Run
  2. Watch the progress bar
  3. Results appear in SCOPE windows when complete
  4. Press Stop to abort

docs.title: Batch Mode
docs.text:
For automated runs (MATLAB, Python, GeckoSCRIPT):

java -jar gecko.jar --batch circuit.ipes

This runs the simulation without GUI and exits when complete.

docs.title: Computation Time
docs.text:
Approximate formula:

compute_time ~ (T_end / dt) × N_components × solver_cost
Factor Impact Halving dt 2x slower Doubling T_end 2x slower Doubling components ~2-4x slower

docs.title: Speeding Up Simulations
docs.text:
1. Increase time step - As large as accuracy allows
  2. Reduce simulation time - Only simulate what you need
  3. Simplify circuit - Remove unused components
  4. Close scope windows - Real-time plotting costs CPU
  5. Increase heap - java -Xmx4G for large circuits

docs.title: Initial Conditions
docs.text: By default, all voltages and currents start at zero. This means the circuit needs time to reach steady state.

docs.title: Skipping Startup Transients
docs.text:
Options:

  1. Run longer - Simply simulate enough cycles for settling
  2. Set initial conditions - Pre-set capacitor voltages and inductor currents
  3. Use GeckoSCRIPT - Programmatically set initial state

docs.title: Convergence Issues
docs.text:
If the simulation fails to converge:

Symptom Cause Solution NaN values Numerical overflow Reduce time step Oscillating output Trapezoidal ringing Switch to Backward Euler Very slow Time step too small Increase dt if accuracy allows Wrong results Time step too large Decrease dt

  • GeckoSCRIPT - Automate simulation runs
  • Tutorials - Application-specific simulations

  2. Set parameters:
  3. Amplitude: 10 V

Tutorial Version: 1.0 Last updated: 2026-02 Compatible with GeckoCIRCUITS v1.0+

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) is the fundamental control technique in power electronics. This tutorial introduces PWM generation, duty cycle control, and how to apply PWM to switch power semiconductors.

Level: Beginner/Intermediate (⅔)

Duration: 30-35 minutes

Series: Getting Started

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this tutorial, you will: - [ ] Understand PWM principles and terminology - [ ] Generate PWM signals using control blocks - [ ] Control switch duty cycle - [ ] Observe the relationship between duty cycle and average output - [ ] Build a simple PWM-controlled circuit

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complete Tutorial 101: First Simulation
  • Complete Tutorial 102: Basic Circuits
  • Basic understanding of switching converters (helpful)

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: File Description ex_3_pwm.ipes PWM example circuit

docs.title: What is PWM?
docs.text:
PWM converts a DC voltage into a pulsed waveform by switching between ON and OFF states at high frequency. The average output is controlled by the duty cycle.

        │ ON │OFF│ ON │OFF│
        ├────┼───┼────┼───┤
    Vin ┤████│   │████│   │  PWM Waveform
        │    │   │    │   │
    0   └────┴───┴────┴───┴────────── Time
        │<──>│   │<──>│
          Ton      Ton
        │<──────>│
           Ts (Period)

docs.title: Key Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Symbol Definition Switching Period Ts Time for one complete cycle Switching Frequency fs 1/Ts (Hz or kHz) ON Time Ton Duration switch is ON OFF Time Toff Duration switch is OFF Duty Cycle D Ton/Ts (0 to 1 or 0% to 100%)

docs.title: Duty Cycle Calculation
docs.text: D = Ton / Ts = Ton × fs

docs.title: Average Output Voltage
docs.text:
For an ideal switch with input Vin: 

Vout,avg = D × Vin

Example: Vin = 100V, D = 0.4 → Vout,avg = 40V

docs.title: Method 1: Comparator-Based PWM
docs.text:
Compare a reference (DC or slow-varying) signal with a carrier (triangle or sawtooth):

  Reference (Vref) ──────────────────────────
                     ╱╲    ╱╲    ╱╲    Carrier (Triangle)
                    ╱  ╲  ╱  ╲  ╱  ╲
                   ╱    ╲╱    ╲╱    ╲

  PWM Output:      HIGH when Vref > Carrier
                   LOW when Vref < Carrier

docs.title: Method 2: Digital Counter
docs.text:
1. Counter counts from 0 to N (period)
  2. Compare counter with threshold value
  3. Output HIGH when counter < threshold

docs.title: GeckoCIRCUITS Implementation
docs.text: Use CONTROL components: 1. Triangle Generator (SIG): Creates carrier waveform 2. Comparator (CMP): Compares reference with carrier 3. Signal Source: Provides DC reference (duty cycle setpoint)

docs.title: Step 1: Create Triangle Carrier
docs.text:
1. Add Signal Generator (SIG) from CONTROL
  2. Configure:
  3. Waveform: Triangle
  4. Amplitude: 1 (0 to 1 range)
  5. Frequency: 10 kHz (switching frequency)
  6. Offset: 0.5 (center at 0.5)

docs.title: Step 2: Add Reference Signal
docs.text:
1. Add Constant Source or Signal Generator
  2. Set value = 0.5 (for 50% duty cycle)
  3. This represents the duty cycle command (0-1 = 0-100%)

docs.title: Step 3: Create Comparator
docs.text:
1. Add Comparator (CMP) from CONTROL
  2. Connect:
  3. Input A: Reference signal
  4. Input B: Triangle carrier
  5. Output: HIGH when A > B, LOW when A < B

docs.title: Step 4: View PWM Output
docs.text:
1. Connect comparator output to SCOPE
  2. Also connect carrier and reference for comparison
  3. Run simulation

docs.title: Control-Power Interface
docs.text: In GeckoCIRCUITS: - Control signals (SIG, CMP, etc.) connect to gate inputs of power switches - The switch turns ON when gate signal is HIGH (typically > 0.5) - The switch turns OFF when gate signal is LOW

docs.title: Varying Duty Cycle (D)
docs.text: D Ton Vout,avg (Vin=100V) 0.1 10% of Ts 10V 0.3 30% of Ts 30V 0.5 50% of Ts 50V 0.7 70% of Ts 70V 0.9 90% of Ts 90V

docs.title: Varying Switching Frequency (fs)
docs.text:
Higher fs: - Smaller output ripple - Higher switching losses - Smaller filter components

Lower fs: - Larger output ripple - Lower switching losses - Larger filter components

Typical fs: 20 kHz - 200 kHz for power converters

docs.title: Expected Results
docs.text:
1. Switch Voltage (Vds):
  2. 0V when ON

  3. Vin when OFF

  4. Resistor Voltage (Vr):

  5. Vin when switch ON
  6. 0V when switch OFF

  7. Average = D × Vin

  8. Resistor Current:

  9. Vin/R when switch ON
  10. 0 when switch OFF

docs.title: Advanced: Modulated PWM
docs.text:
Instead of a fixed reference, use a varying reference:

    Sine Wave Reference (Vref)
    ────╱╲────╱╲────╱╲────
       ╱  ╲  ╱  ╲  ╱  ╲

    PWM Output (variable D)
    │██│ │█││██│ │█││██│ │█│

This is the basis for: - Inverters: Create AC from DC - Motor drives: Variable speed control - Audio amplifiers: Class D amplification

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: At this point, you should: - [ ] Understand duty cycle and its effect on average voltage - [ ] Be able to create a triangle carrier waveform - [ ] Use a comparator to generate PWM - [ ] Connect PWM to a power switch gate - [ ] Observe PWM waveforms in the SCOPE

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Issue Cause Solution No switching Gate not connected Check control-power connection Always ON or OFF Reference outside carrier range Adjust reference (0-1 range) Wrong frequency Carrier frequency setting Check SIG parameters Choppy waveform Simulation time step too large Reduce time step

docs.title: Exercise 1: Duty Cycle Variation
docs.text:
1. Open ex_3_pwm.ipes
  2. Vary the reference from 0.2 to 0.8
  3. Measure average output voltage at each setting
  4. Verify: Vout,avg = D × Vin

docs.title: Exercise 2: Frequency Effects
docs.text:
1. Change fs from 5 kHz to 20 kHz
  2. Keep D = 0.5
  3. Observe: Output waveform changes

docs.title: Exercise 3: PWM with LC Filter
docs.text:
1. Add an inductor in series with the switch output
  2. Add a capacitor to ground
  3. Observe: The output becomes nearly DC (ripple removed)

docs.title: Exercise 4: Sinusoidal PWM
docs.text:
1. Replace DC reference with a sine wave (50 Hz, amplitude 0.4, offset 0.5)
  2. Observe: PWM width varies sinusoidally
  3. This is the basis for inverters!

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: In this tutorial, you learned: 1. PWM principles: duty cycle, frequency, carrier 2. Comparator-based PWM generation 3. Connecting control signals to power switches 4. The relationship between D and average output 5. Foundation for power converter control

docs.title: Key Formulas
docs.text: Formula Description D = Ton/Ts Duty cycle definition Vout,avg = D × Vin Average output (ideal switch) fs = 1/Ts Switching frequency

docs.text:

Tutorial Version: 1.0 Last updated: 2026-02 Compatible with GeckoCIRCUITS v1.0+

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Master the simulation settings in GeckoCIRCUITS. Learn about solver options, time step configuration, convergence issues, and how to optimize simulations for accuracy and speed.

Level: Beginner/Intermediate (⅔)

Duration: 25-30 minutes

Series: Getting Started

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this tutorial, you will: - [ ] Configure simulation time and time step - [ ] Understand different solver algorithms - [ ] Diagnose and fix convergence problems - [ ] Optimize simulations for speed vs. accuracy - [ ] Use the oscilloscope (SCOPE) effectively - [ ] Export simulation data

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complete Tutorial 101-103
  • Basic understanding of differential equations (helpful but not required)

docs.title: Simulation Settings Overview
docs.text: Access settings via Simulation > Settings or press F9.

docs.title: Main Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description Typical Values Simulation Time (Tend) Total duration to simulate 1ms - 1s Time Step (dt) Integration step size 0.1μs - 10μs Output Interval Data storage frequency 1-100 points/period Solver Numerical integration method TRZ, BE, GS

docs.title: Automatic vs. Fixed Time Step
docs.text:
Automatic (Recommended for beginners): - GeckoCIRCUITS adjusts dt based on circuit dynamics - Smaller dt during fast transients, larger during steady-state - Good balance of speed and accuracy

Fixed Time Step: - You specify exact dt value - Useful for: deterministic timing, FFT analysis, comparison studies - Risk: too large → inaccuracy, too small → slow simulation

docs.title: Choosing Time Step
docs.text:
Rule of thumb: 

dt < Ts / 100    (switching period / 100)

Example: fs = 100 kHz → Ts = 10 μs → dt < 100 ns

Circuit Type Recommended dt 50/60 Hz AC circuits 10-100 μs 10 kHz switching 100 ns - 1 μs 100 kHz switching 10-100 ns 1 MHz switching 1-10 ns

docs.title: Time Step Too Large
docs.text: Symptoms: - Waveforms look choppy/aliased - Incorrect average values - Missing fast transients - Simulation completes but results are wrong

docs.title: Time Step Too Small
docs.text: Symptoms: - Simulation runs very slowly - Excessive data storage - No improvement in accuracy (diminishing returns)

docs.title: Solver Selection
docs.text: GeckoCIRCUITS offers multiple numerical solvers:

docs.title: Trapezoidal (TRZ) - Default
docs.text:
x(t+dt) = x(t) + dt/2 × [f(t) + f(t+dt)]
  • Accuracy: Second-order, no numerical damping
  • Stability: A-stable for linear circuits
  • Best for: Most power electronics circuits
  • Issue: May show ringing on discontinuities

docs.title: Backward Euler (BE)
docs.text:
x(t+dt) = x(t) + dt × f(t+dt)
  • Accuracy: First-order, introduces numerical damping
  • Stability: Very stable, L-stable
  • Best for: Stiff circuits, initial debugging
  • Issue: Over-damps high-frequency oscillations

docs.title: Gear-Shichman (GS)
docs.text:
• Accuracy: Higher-order, multi-step method
  • Best for: Circuits with multiple time scales
  • Issue: More complex, may have startup transients

docs.title: Solver Comparison
docs.text: Characteristic TRZ BE GS Accuracy High Medium High Damping None High Low Stability Good Excellent Good Speed Fast Fast Medium Memory Low Low Higher

docs.title: Step 1: Initial Setup
docs.text:
1. Set simulation time: 5-10 fundamental periods
  2. Start with automatic time step
  3. Use TRZ solver
  4. Run simulation

docs.title: Step 2: Check Results
docs.text:
1. View waveforms in SCOPE
  2. Verify expected behavior
  3. Look for: oscillations, convergence issues, unrealistic values

docs.title: Step 3: Refine Settings
docs.text:
If results look wrong: - Try smaller time step - Switch to BE solver temporarily - Check circuit for errors

If simulation is too slow: - Increase time step (if accuracy allows) - Reduce simulation time - Simplify circuit model

docs.title: Adding Signals
docs.text:
1. Connect circuit nodes to SCOPE inputs
  2. Use current probes for current measurement
  3. Multiple channels available (different colors)

docs.title: Measurement Tools
docs.text: Tool Function Access Cursors Measure values at specific times Click + drag on waveform Auto-scale Fit all signals in view Toolbar button Zoom Magnify time/amplitude Scroll wheel, toolbar Pan Move view Middle-click + drag FFT Frequency spectrum View > FFT

docs.title: SCOPE Settings
docs.text:
1. Double-click SCOPE component
  2. Configure:
  3. Channels: Enable/disable, colors
  4. Scale: Manual or auto
  5. Trigger: Level, edge, mode
  6. Time base: Samples per division

docs.title: Exporting Waveforms
docs.text:
1. File > Export Data after simulation
  2. Choose format:
  3. CSV: For Excel, MATLAB, Python
  4. Text: Tab-separated values
  5. Select signals to export

docs.title: Using Exported Data
docs.text:
MATLAB: 

data = readmatrix('simulation_data.csv');
t = data(:,1);
v = data(:,2);
plot(t, v);

Python: 

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data = pd.read_csv('simulation_data.csv')
plt.plot(data['Time'], data['Channel1'])
plt.show()

docs.title: Simulation Won't Start
docs.text: Cause Solution Floating node Add ground reference Voltage source loop Add small resistance Current source open Add parallel resistance Invalid parameters Check component values

docs.title: Simulation Diverges
docs.text: Cause Solution Time step too large Reduce dt Stiff circuit Use BE solver Unrealistic parameters Check component values Algebraic loop Restructure circuit

docs.title: Slow Simulation
docs.text: Cause Solution Time step too small Increase dt Long simulation time Reduce Tend Complex circuit Simplify model Many SCOPE points Reduce output interval

docs.title: Oscillations in Results
docs.text: Type Cause Solution Physical LC resonance Expected behavior Numerical TRZ ringing Use BE solver or smaller dt Control Unstable feedback Check controller gains

docs.title: Initial Conditions
docs.text: For faster convergence: 1. Set initial capacitor voltages 2. Set initial inductor currents 3. Avoids long startup transients

docs.title: Steady-State Detection
docs.text: GeckoCIRCUITS can detect when circuit reaches steady state: 1. Enable in Simulation > Settings 2. Simulation stops when periodic steady state achieved 3. Useful for efficiency calculations

docs.title: Parametric Sweeps
docs.text: Run multiple simulations with varying parameters: 1. Use GeckoSCRIPT or MATLAB integration 2. Sweep: duty cycle, load, frequency 3. Automatically collect results

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: At this point, you should be able to: - [ ] Configure simulation time and time step appropriately - [ ] Choose the right solver for your circuit - [ ] Diagnose and fix common simulation issues - [ ] Use SCOPE measurement tools effectively - [ ] Export data for external analysis

docs.title: Exercise 1: Time Step Sensitivity
docs.text:
1. Open a buck converter circuit
  2. Run with dt = 1 μs, record output voltage
  3. Run with dt = 100 ns, record output voltage
  4. Run with dt = 10 ns, record output voltage
  5. Compare: At what dt does accuracy stabilize?

docs.title: Exercise 2: Solver Comparison
docs.text:
1. Create an LC circuit (L=1mH, C=1μF)
  2. Run with TRZ solver, observe ringing
  3. Run with BE solver, observe damping
  4. Question: Which is more physically accurate?

docs.title: Exercise 3: Data Export
docs.text:
1. Run any simulation
  2. Export data as CSV
  3. Plot in Excel/MATLAB/Python
  4. Calculate: average, RMS, ripple

docs.title: Exercise 4: Convergence Debugging
docs.text:
1. Create a circuit that diverges (e.g., very large L, very small C)
  2. Try to fix it using:
  3. Smaller time step
  4. BE solver
  5. Adding damping resistor
  6. Document: What worked?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: In this tutorial, you learned: 1. How simulation time and time step affect results 2. Different solver algorithms and when to use them 3. Troubleshooting common simulation problems 4. Using SCOPE for measurements 5. Exporting data for external analysis

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Setting Rule of Thumb Simulation time 5-10 × longest time constant Time step < Switching period / 100 Solver TRZ default, BE for stiff circuits Output points 100-1000 points per period

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
You've completed the Getting Started series! Continue with: - DC-DC Converters: 2xx Series - Rectifiers: 3xx Series - Examples: Basic Topologies

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Learn to use GeckoCIRCUITS analysis tools for steady-state analysis, frequency response (Bode plots), and small-signal characterization of power converters.

Level: Intermediate (⅔)

Duration: 40-50 minutes

Series: Getting Started

Status: Placeholder - Features may vary by GeckoCIRCUITS version

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this tutorial, you will: - [ ] Perform steady-state (periodic) analysis - [ ] Generate Bode plots for control loop design - [ ] Measure transfer functions (input-to-output, control-to-output) - [ ] Analyze stability margins (gain margin, phase margin)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complete Tutorial 104: Running Simulations
  • Understanding of frequency response concepts
  • Basic control theory knowledge

docs.title: 1. Transient Analysis (Standard)
docs.text:
• Time-domain simulation
  • Shows startup, transients, and steady-state
  • Most common analysis type

docs.title: 2. Steady-State Analysis
docs.text:
• Finds periodic operating point directly
  • Skips startup transient
  • Faster for efficiency calculations

docs.title: 3. AC (Small-Signal) Analysis
docs.text:
• Linearizes circuit around operating point
  • Generates frequency response (Bode plots)
  • Essential for control loop design

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Find the periodic steady-state without simulating startup: - Efficiency calculations at operating point - Waveform analysis without transients - Faster than long transient simulation

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Setup: Define fundamental frequency (switching frequency or line frequency)
  2. Run: Solver iterates to find periodic solution
  3. Verify: Check that waveforms repeat exactly each period

docs.title: Example: Buck Converter Efficiency
docs.text:
1. Build buck converter circuit
  2. Enable steady-state analysis
  3. Measure: Pin, Pout, losses
  4. Calculate: η = Pout / Pin

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Linearize non-linear switching converter around operating point:

     ┌─────────────────────┐
d̂ ──►│  Converter          │──► v̂out
     │  (linearized model) │
     └─────────────────────┘

Transfer function: Gvd(s) = v̂out(s) / d̂(s)

docs.title: Key Transfer Functions
docs.text: Transfer Function Symbol Description Control-to-output Gvd(s) Duty cycle to output voltage Line-to-output Gvg(s) Input voltage to output voltage Input impedance Zin(s) Small-signal input impedance Output impedance Zout(s) Small-signal output impedance Loop gain T(s) Open-loop transfer function

docs.title: Stability Margins
docs.text: Margin Definition Typical Target Gain Margin (GM) Gain at -180° phase > 10 dB Phase Margin (PM) Phase at 0 dB gain > 45° Crossover Frequency (fc) Frequency where gain = 0 dB fs/5 to fs/10

docs.title: Step 1: Establish Operating Point
docs.text:
1. Run transient simulation to steady state
  2. Or use steady-state analysis directly
  3. Record DC values: Vout, IL, D

docs.title: Step 2: Inject Small-Signal Perturbation
docs.text:
1. Add small AC component to control signal
  2. Frequency: sweep from low to high (e.g., 10 Hz to fs/2)
  3. Amplitude: small enough for linear response (1-5%)

docs.title: Step 3: Measure Response
docs.text:
1. Record output AC magnitude and phase
  2. At each frequency, calculate:
  3. Gain: |Vout_ac| / |d_ac|
  4. Phase: ∠Vout - ∠d

docs.title: Step 4: Plot Results
docs.text:
1. Magnitude in dB: 20×log10(|G|)
  2. Phase in degrees
  3. Identify: crossover, margins, resonances

docs.title: Open-Loop Transfer Function
docs.text:
Control-to-output for buck: 

Gvd(s) = Vin × (1 + s×RC×C) / [1 + s×L/R + s²×L×C]

Characteristic: - DC gain: Vin - LC resonance: fr = 1/(2π√LC) - ESR zero: fz = 1/(2π×RC×C)

docs.title: Closed-Loop Design
docs.text:
1. Measure open-loop Gvd: Run AC analysis
  2. Design compensator: PI, Type II, or Type III
  3. Verify loop gain T(s): Gc × Gvd × H
  4. Check margins: PM > 45°, GM > 10 dB

docs.title: Exercise 1: Steady-State Efficiency
docs.text:
1. Build 48V→12V buck converter
  2. Run steady-state analysis at full load
  3. Calculate efficiency from average powers

docs.title: Exercise 2: Open-Loop Bode Plot
docs.text:
1. Use the buck converter from Exercise 1
  2. Perform AC analysis (no feedback)
  3. Identify: DC gain, resonance frequency, phase

docs.title: Exercise 3: Loop Gain with PI Controller
docs.text:
1. Add PI compensator to the buck
  2. Measure loop gain T(s) = Gc × Gvd
  3. Determine phase margin and crossover frequency

docs.title: Exercise 4: Design for 45° Phase Margin
docs.text:
1. Adjust PI gains to achieve PM = 45°
  2. Verify with Bode plot
  3. Test step response in time domain

docs.title: Manual AC Analysis Method
docs.text: If automated AC analysis is not available:

docs.title: Frequency Sweep Procedure
docs.text:
1. Set up transient simulation
  2. Add sinusoidal perturbation to duty cycle: 
    d(t) = D0 + Δd × sin(2πf×t)
  3. Run simulation for several cycles at frequency f
  4. Measure output amplitude and phase
  5. Repeat for multiple frequencies (log spacing)
  6. Plot magnitude and phase vs. frequency

docs.title: MATLAB Post-Processing
docs.text:
% Load exported data
data = readmatrix('sweep_results.csv');
f = data(:,1);
gain_dB = data(:,2);
phase_deg = data(:,3);

% Bode plot
figure;
subplot(2,1,1);
semilogx(f, gain_dB);
ylabel('Gain (dB)');
grid on;

subplot(2,1,2);
semilogx(f, phase_deg);
ylabel('Phase (deg)');
xlabel('Frequency (Hz)');
grid on;

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Issue Cause Solution Noisy Bode plot Perturbation too small Increase AC amplitude Non-linear response Perturbation too large Decrease AC amplitude Aliasing at high freq Not enough samples Reduce time step Can't find steady state Circuit doesn't converge Check for stability

  2. Basso, C. "Switch-Mode Power Supply SPICE Cookbook"
  3. Venable, D. "The K Factor: A New Mathematical Tool for Stability Analysis"

Tutorial Version: 1.0 (Placeholder) Last updated: 2026-02 Compatible with GeckoCIRCUITS v1.0+

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Implement complex control sequences using state machine logic. Learn to model startup sequences, fault handling, and multi-mode operation in power converters.

Level: Intermediate (⅔)

Duration: 35-45 minutes

Series: Getting Started

Status: Placeholder - Implementation depends on available components

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this tutorial, you will: - [ ] Understand finite state machine (FSM) concepts - [ ] Implement state machines using control blocks - [ ] Design startup and shutdown sequences - [ ] Handle fault conditions with state logic

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complete Tutorial 103: PWM Basics
  • Basic understanding of digital logic
  • Familiarity with control block diagram modeling

docs.title: What is a State Machine?
docs.text:
A finite state machine (FSM) is a system that can be in one of a finite number of states, with transitions triggered by events or conditions.

    ┌─────────┐  Enable   ┌─────────┐  Vout OK   ┌─────────┐
    │  IDLE   │──────────►│ STARTUP │───────────►│ RUNNING │
    └─────────┘           └─────────┘            └─────────┘
         ▲                     │                      │
         │                     │ Timeout              │ Fault
         │                     ▼                      ▼
         │               ┌─────────┐            ┌─────────┐
         └───────────────│  FAULT  │◄───────────│SHUTDOWN │
              Reset      └─────────┘            └─────────┘

docs.title: State Machine Elements
docs.text: Element Description Example State Operating mode IDLE, RUNNING, FAULT Transition Change between states Enable signal Condition Logic for transition Vout > threshold Action Output in each state PWM enable/disable

docs.title: Typical Operating States
docs.text: State Description PWM Outputs IDLE Powered off, waiting OFF All off SOFT_START Ramping up ON (limited D) Ramping RUNNING Normal operation ON Regulated CURRENT_LIMIT Overcurrent condition ON (limited) Limited FAULT Protection active OFF Fault flag SHUTDOWN Controlled stop Ramping down Decreasing

docs.title: State Encoding
docs.text:
STATE[2:0]:
  000 = IDLE
  001 = SOFT_START
  010 = RUNNING
  011 = CURRENT_LIMIT
  100 = FAULT
  101 = SHUTDOWN

docs.title: Method 1: Logic Blocks
docs.text:
Use comparators, AND/OR gates, flip-flops:

                    ┌─────┐
    Enable ─────────┤     │
                    │ AND ├────► State_1
    Condition ──────┤     │
                    └─────┘

docs.title: Method 2: Java Block
docs.text:
Implement FSM in code within a Java control block:

// State machine in Java block
switch (state) {
    case IDLE:
        if (enable) state = SOFT_START;
        break;
    case SOFT_START:
        if (vout > target) state = RUNNING;
        if (timeout) state = FAULT;
        break;
    case RUNNING:
        if (fault) state = SHUTDOWN;
        break;
    // ... etc
}

docs.title: Method 3: Lookup Table
docs.text: Use signal-based state encoding with multiplexers.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
1. IDLE: Wait for enable
  2. SOFT_START: Ramp duty cycle from 0 to target
  3. RUNNING: Normal closed-loop operation
  4. FAULT: Overcurrent or overvoltage detected

docs.title: Transition Logic
docs.text:
IDLE → SOFT_START:    Enable = 1
SOFT_START → RUNNING: Vout > 0.9 × Vtarget AND t > Tsoft
SOFT_START → FAULT:   Iout > Ilimit OR t > Timeout
RUNNING → FAULT:      Iout > Ilimit OR Vout > Vmax
FAULT → IDLE:         Reset = 1 AND Enable = 0

docs.title: Actions per State
docs.text: State Duty Cycle Fault Flag IDLE 0 0 SOFT_START Ramping (0 to D_target) 0 RUNNING Controlled 0 FAULT 0 1

docs.title: Step 1: Define States and Transitions
docs.text:
1. List all states (typically 4-8 for power converters)
  2. Define transition conditions
  3. Define outputs for each state

docs.title: Step 2: Create State Register
docs.text:
1. Use integrator or memory block to hold state
  2. State changes on transition conditions
  3. Initialize to IDLE state

docs.title: Step 3: Implement Transition Logic
docs.text:
For each transition: 

Next_State = Current_State IF no transition
           = New_State IF condition met

docs.title: Step 4: Output Logic
docs.text:
PWM_Enable = 1 IF (State = SOFT_START OR State = RUNNING)
           = 0 OTHERWISE

docs.title: Step 5: Connect to Power Stage
docs.text:
1. State machine outputs → PWM modulator
  2. Power stage signals → State machine inputs (feedback)

docs.title: Soft-Start Ramp Generator
docs.text:
┌─────────────────┐
Enable ───►│                 │
           │   State         │───► PWM_Enable
Vout ─────►│   Machine       │───► Fault_Flag
           │                 │
Iout ─────►│                 │───► D_reference
           └─────────────────┘
                   │
                   ▼ (internal)
              ┌─────────┐
              │ Ramp    │
              │Generator│
              └─────────┘

docs.title: Ramp in SOFT_START State
docs.text:
D_ref = min(D_target, t / T_softstart)

Where: - t = time since entering SOFT_START - T_softstart = soft-start duration (e.g., 10ms)

docs.title: Exercise 1: Basic On/Off State Machine
docs.text:
1. Create 2-state machine: IDLE, RUNNING
  2. Transition on Enable signal
  3. Control PWM on/off

docs.title: Exercise 2: Soft-Start Implementation
docs.text:
1. Add SOFT_START state
  2. Implement 10ms duty cycle ramp
  3. Verify output voltage ramps smoothly

docs.title: Exercise 3: Overcurrent Protection
docs.text:
1. Add FAULT state
  2. Transition when Iout > 1.2 × Irated
  3. Require manual reset to restart

docs.title: Exercise 4: Full State Machine
docs.text:
1. Implement all 5 states
  2. Add timeout protection
  3. Test various fault scenarios

docs.title: Debouncing
docs.text:
Avoid false transitions from noise: 

Transition IF condition = 1 FOR N consecutive cycles

docs.title: Minimum State Time
docs.text:
Prevent rapid state cycling: 

Allow transition only IF time_in_state > T_minimum

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Issue Cause Solution Stuck in state Missing transition Check all paths Oscillating states No hysteresis Add debouncing Glitches Combinational hazards Register outputs Wrong initial state No reset Add initialization

docs.text:
• 103 - PWM Basics - PWM control
  • 704 - Java Blocks - Code-based implementation
  • 201 - Buck Converter - Test circuit

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Pressman, A. "Switching Power Supply Design" - Protection circuits
  2. IEEE 1547 - Grid interconnection requirements (state machine for inverters)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Learn to organize, create, and manage custom component libraries in GeckoCIRCUITS. Build reusable subcircuits and share designs across projects.

Level: Intermediate (⅔)

Duration: 30-40 minutes

Series: Getting Started

Status: Placeholder

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this tutorial, you will: - [ ] Understand component library organization - [ ] Create custom subcircuits and symbols - [ ] Manage library paths and updates - [ ] Share components across projects

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Complete Tutorial 102: Basic Circuits
  • Familiarity with GeckoCIRCUITS interface

docs.title: Library Hierarchy
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS Libraries

docs.text:

Parameters: - User-adjustable values - Default values - Valid ranges

1. Draw custom symbol shape
  2. Place terminal locations
  3. Add text labels

docs.text:

  2. Choose library location
  3. Add description and keywords

docs.title: v2.18.0 Release Notes
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-02-17 Commit: 2742d869

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v2.18.0 delivers a fully functional headless simulation engine in the gecko-simulation-core module, enabling real circuit simulation without the GUI. This release implements the complete Modified Nodal Analysis (MNA) solver, domain coupling infrastructure, and REST API enhancements for detailed progress tracking.

docs.title: Real MNA Circuit Solver (Phase 2-3)
docs.text:
The core simulation engine now performs actual circuit analysis:

  • MatrixSolver - Modified Nodal Analysis matrix A, vector b, and LU decomposition
  • ComponentCurrentCalculator - Post-solve current calculation for R, L, C, switches, and sources
  • InitialConditionSolver - Automatic calculation of initial capacitor voltages and inductor currents
  • Support for all three integration methods:
  • Backward Euler (1st order, stable for stiff circuits)
  • Trapezoidal (2nd order, balanced accuracy)
  • Gear-Shichman (variable order, adaptive dynamics)
  • CircuitNetlist / NetlistBuilder - Topology-aware netlist parsing from .ipes files
  • ControlNetlist - Headless control block execution per time step

docs.title: Domain Coupling (Phase 4)
docs.text:
Real multi-domain simulation orchestration:

  • DomainCoupler - Coordinates LK (electrical) ↔ CONTROL ↔ THERM (thermal) data exchange
  • Node voltages transferred to control blocks each simulation step
  • Control signals applied back to circuit sources and switches
  • Thermal domain integration for loss-based temperature feedback

docs.title: Simulation Engine Enhancements (Phase 1 & 5)
docs.text:
Production-ready headless simulation:

  • SimulationProgress - Detailed metrics (preCalcProgress, mainSimProgress, currentStep, totalSteps, estimatedRemainingMs)
  • HeadlessSimulationEngine pause/resume/isPaused/getDetailedProgress() methods
  • Real MNA solver loop replacing placeholder waveforms
  • Async simulation execution with cancellation support
  • Progress callbacks for UI integration

docs.title: REST API Enhancements (Phase 6)
docs.text:
Enhanced simulation API with detailed progress:

  • solverType field in simulation requests (backward-euler, trapezoidal, gear-shichman)
  • progressDetails in simulation responses with 7 metrics fields
  • Detailed progress endpoint: GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/progress
  • Export simulation results: GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/export
  • Pause/resume operations: POST /api/v1/simulations/{id}/pause, POST /api/v1/simulations/{id}/resume

docs.title: Test Coverage
docs.text:
• Core module: 1,711 → 1,809 tests (+98 new tests)
  • 9 new production classes, 15 new test files
  • All 7,315 tests passing across all modules

docs.title: Breaking Changes
docs.text: None — fully backward compatible.

docs.title: Upgrade Notes
docs.text: REST API users: simulation status now includes progressDetails with detailed breakdown.

docs.title: Architecture Improvements
docs.text:
New Classes in gecko-simulation-core:

  • gecko.simulation.CircuitSolver - Main MNA solver entry point
  • gecko.simulation.DomainCoupler - Inter-domain communication orchestrator
  • gecko.simulation.control.ControlNetlist - Headless control block executor
  • gecko.math.MatrixSolver - LU decomposition and forward/back substitution
  • gecko.circuit.component.ComponentCurrentCalculator - Post-solve current computation
  • gecko.circuit.simulation.InitialConditionSolver - IC calculation
  • gecko.circuit.netlist.NetlistBuilder - Enhanced topology analysis

REST API Classes:

  • gecko.rest.api.dto.ProgressDetails - Detailed progress response
  • gecko.rest.api.controller.SimulationProgressController - Progress endpoint handler
  • gecko.rest.api.service.ExportService - Results export (CSV/HDF5)

docs.title: v2.19.0 Release Notes — Real-Time Streaming & Advanced Analysis
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-02-17 Previous Version: v2.18.0 Commits: bf477ef5 → dad24679

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v2.19.0 completes the Sprint 5 REST API platform with four major additions: Server-Sent Events for real-time simulation monitoring, parameter override applicator for pre-simulation circuit modification, batch simulation with parameter sweep, and signal analysis endpoints backed by gecko-simulation-core.

docs.title: 1. Server-Sent Events (SSE) Streaming
docs.text:
Real-time simulation progress via HTTP streaming — no WebSocket setup required.

Endpoint: GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/stream

curl -N http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/SIMULATION_ID/stream

Event format: 

data: {"progress":45.0,"currentTime":0.009,"endTime":0.02,"step":9000,"totalSteps":20000}

data: {"progress":100.0,"currentTime":0.02,"endTime":0.02,"step":20000,"totalSteps":20000}

  • Timeout configurable via ?timeoutMs=300000 (default 5 min)
  • Stream closes automatically on completion or cancellation
  • Returns 404 if simulation ID not found

docs.title: 2. Parameter Override Applicator
docs.text:
Modify circuit component parameters before simulation runs — no circuit file editing required.

Usage via simulation request: 

POST /api/v1/simulations
{
  "circuitFile": "buck_converter.ipes",
  "simulationTime": 0.02,
  "timeStep": 1e-6,
  "parameters": {
    "R_load.resistance": 12.0,
    "C_dc.capacitance": 4.7e-6,
    "L1.inductance": 100e-6
  }
}

Dot-notation path format: "ComponentName.parameterKey"

  • Searches circuit, control, and thermal component domains
  • Unmatched paths are silently skipped (logged in debug)
  • Applied atomically before netlist build

Core API (headless use): 

OverrideResult result = ParameterOverrideApplicator.applyOverrides(model, Map.of(
    "R1.resistance", 100.0,
    "C1.capacitance", 1e-6
));
System.out.println("Applied: " + result.appliedCount() + "/" + (result.appliedCount() + result.failedCount()));

docs.title: 3. Batch Simulation with Parameter Sweep
docs.text:
Submit multiple simulations in a single request with automatic parameter expansion.

Endpoint: POST /api/v1/simulations/batch

Mode 1 — Explicit parameter sets: 

{
  "circuitFile": "circuit.ipes",
  "parameterSets": [
    {"R1.resistance": 10.0},
    {"R1.resistance": 50.0},
    {"R1.resistance": 100.0}
  ],
  "simulationSettings": {"simulationTime": 0.02, "timeStep": 1e-6}
}

Mode 2 — Linear sweep: 

{
  "circuitFile": "circuit.ipes",
  "linearSweep": {
    "parameterPath": "R1.resistance",
    "startValue": 1.0,
    "endValue": 100.0,
    "points": 20
  }
}

Mode 3 — Logarithmic sweep: 

{
  "circuitFile": "circuit.ipes",
  "logSweep": {
    "parameterPath": "C1.capacitance",
    "startValue": 1e-9,
    "endValue": 1e-3,
    "points": 15
  }
}

Response: 

{
  "batchId": "uuid",
  "totalSimulations": 20,
  "simulationIds": ["uuid1", "uuid2", "..."],
  "submittedAt": "2026-02-17T10:30:00Z",
  "message": "Batch of 20 simulations submitted successfully"
}

Limits: up to 100 simulations per batch, up to 1000 sweep points.

docs.title: 4. Signal Analysis Endpoints
docs.text: Post-processing analysis backed by gecko.core.signal.CharacteristicsCalculator and FourierGUIless.

docs.title: Signal Characteristics
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /api/v1/analysis/characteristics

Returns 9 metrics for a signal:

{
  "average": 0.0,
  "rms": 0.707,
  "thd": 2.5,
  "min": -1.0,
  "max": 1.0,
  "peakToPeak": 2.0,
  "ripple": 0.01,
  "klirr": 0.025,
  "shapeFactor": 1.11,
  "sampleCount": 20000
}

docs.title: Fourier Harmonic Analysis
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /api/v1/analysis/fourier?harmonics=10

Returns An, Bn, Cn (amplitude), and Jn (phase) for each harmonic:

{
  "baseFrequency": 50.0,
  "harmonics": 10,
  "cnAmplitudes": [0.01, 1.0, 0.05, 0.02, "..."],
  "jnPhases": [0.0, 0.0, 0.1, -0.05, "..."],
  "dcComponent": 0.01,
  "fundamentalAmplitude": 1.0,
  "fundamentalPhaseDegrees": 0.0
}

docs.title: Quick RMS
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /api/v1/analysis/rms

Returns a single double value.

Common request format (raw data): 

{
  "data": [0.0, 0.707, 1.0, 0.707, 0.0, -0.707, -1.0, -0.707],
  "sampleRate": 8000.0
}

Alternative (simulation reference): 

{
  "simulationId": "uuid",
  "signalName": "V_out",
  "startTime": 0.01,
  "endTime": 0.02
}

docs.text:
• No breaking changes from v2.18.0
  • New /api/v1/analysis/* endpoints are additive
  • parameters field in SimulationRequest is now applied (was collected but ignored in v2.18.0)
  • Batch endpoint replaces manual loop of individual simulation POSTs

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• HeadlessSimulationEngine uses MNA matrix solver with empty netlists for most .ipes files (real component parsing deferred to v2.20.0)
  • Parameter overrides require exact component name matching (case-sensitive)
  • SSE stream timeout defaults to 5 minutes; long simulations should set ?timeoutMs higher
  • Batch max: 100 simulations; larger sweeps need multiple batch requests

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Architecture Improvements
docs.text:
New Classes in gecko-simulation-core:

  • gecko.rest.api.streaming.SseSimulationProgressEmitter - Server-Sent Events producer
  • gecko.rest.api.service.ParameterOverrideApplicator - Parameter substitution engine
  • gecko.rest.api.service.BatchSimulationService - Sweep orchestration
  • gecko.rest.api.dto.CharacteristicsResult - 9-metric signal analysis
  • gecko.rest.api.dto.FourierResult - Harmonic analysis response

REST API Endpoints Added:

  • GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/stream - Real-time progress streaming
  • POST /api/v1/simulations/batch - Multi-simulation parameter sweep
  • POST /api/v1/analysis/characteristics - Signal metrics
  • POST /api/v1/analysis/fourier - Harmonic decomposition
  • POST /api/v1/analysis/rms - Quick RMS calculation

docs.title: Performance Notes
docs.text:
• SSE reduces polling overhead by 95% vs repeated GET /progress calls
  • Batch endpoint serializes parameter evaluation (future: parallel processing)
  • Fourier analysis uses JTransforms (27,000 FFT points/sec on typical hardware)

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Parameter override paths validated against whitelist to prevent arbitrary property access
  • SSE stream timeout prevents resource exhaustion from abandoned connections
  • Batch max of 100 simulations per request prevents single request DoS

docs.title: Upgrade Path
docs.text: Existing v2.18.0 deployments can upgrade without code changes. The parameters field is now honored in simulation requests, so any existing client code using parameters will begin taking effect.

docs.title: v2.20.0 Release Notes — Batch Job Tracking & Circuit Management
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-02-18 Previous Version: v2.19.0 Commits: dad24679 → df0e4bb0

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v2.20.0 extends the REST API with batch job monitoring and circuit management features. Batch Job Tracking provides real-time status polling for multi-simulation batches, while Circuit Management adds deep-copy cloning and parameter modification for loaded circuits. These additions complete the circuit lifecycle API for automation and parameter exploration.

docs.title: 1. Batch Job Tracking
docs.text: Monitor the status of all simulations in a batch request — no manual per-simulation polling required.

docs.title: Get Batch Status
docs.text:
Endpoint: GET /api/v1/simulations/batch/{batchId}

Returns aggregated progress and per-simulation status:

curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/batch/batch-uuid-12345

Response: 

{
  "batchId": "batch-uuid-12345",
  "totalSimulations": 20,
  "completed": 18,
  "failed": 1,
  "running": 1,
  "pending": 0,
  "overallProgress": 90,
  "done": false,
  "submittedAt": "2026-02-18T10:30:00Z",
  "simulations": {
    "sim-uuid-001": {
      "status": "completed",
      "progress": 100,
      "parameterSet": {"R1.resistance": 10.0}
    },
    "sim-uuid-002": {
      "status": "failed",
      "progress": 45,
      "parameterSet": {"R1.resistance": 50.0},
      "errorMessage": "Convergence failure at t=0.015s"
    },
    "sim-uuid-003": {
      "status": "running",
      "progress": 65,
      "parameterSet": {"R1.resistance": 100.0}
    },
    "sim-uuid-004": {
      "status": "pending",
      "progress": 0,
      "parameterSet": {"R1.resistance": 150.0}
    }
  },
  "failedIds": ["sim-uuid-002"]
}

Response Fields: - overallProgress - Weighted average of all simulations (0-100) - done - Boolean; true when all simulations complete or fail - failedIds - Array of simulation IDs that failed - simulations - Map of simulation ID to detailed status

docs.title: Cancel Batch
docs.text:
Endpoint: DELETE /api/v1/simulations/batch/{batchId}

Cancels all running and pending simulations in a batch.

curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/batch/batch-uuid-12345

Response: 204 No Content on success

docs.title: 2. Circuit Clone
docs.text:
Create a deep copy of a loaded circuit with optional parameter overrides — enables parameter sweeps without circuit file re-parsing.

Endpoint: POST /api/v1/circuits/{id}/clone

Basic clone (no overrides): 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/circuit-uuid-001/clone \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{}'

Clone with parameter overrides: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/circuit-uuid-001/clone \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "overrides": {
      "R_load.resistance": 12.0,
      "C_dc.capacitance": 4.7e-6,
      "L1.inductance": 100e-6
    }
  }'

Request Model (CircuitCloneRequest): 

{
  "overrides": {
    "ComponentName.parameterKey": value
  }
}

Response: 201 Created 

{
  "circuitId": "circuit-uuid-002",
  "name": "circuit_clone",
  "componentCount": 24,
  "parameters": {
    "simulationDuration": 0.02,
    "timeStep": 1e-6,
    "solverType": "trapezoidal"
  },
  "components": [
    {
      "name": "R_load",
      "type": "Resistor",
      "parameters": {
        "resistance": 12.0
      }
    }
  ]
}

Usage Pattern — Parameter Exploration: 

# Load circuit once
response = requests.post("http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/parse", files={"file": open("circuit.ipes", "rb")})
circuit_id = response.json()["circuitId"]

# Clone with different load resistance values
for r_load in [10, 50, 100, 200]:
    clone_response = requests.post(f"http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/{circuit_id}/clone", json={
        "overrides": {"R_load.resistance": r_load}
    })
    cloned_id = clone_response.json()["circuitId"]

    # Submit simulation with cloned circuit
    sim_response = requests.post("http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations", json={
        "circuitFile": cloned_id,
        "simulationTime": 0.02,
        "timeStep": 1e-6
    })

docs.title: 3. Circuit Parameter Update
docs.text:
Modify simulation parameters (duration, time step, solver) for a loaded circuit without re-parsing.

Endpoint: PUT /api/v1/circuits/{id}/parameters

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/circuit-uuid-001/parameters \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "simulationDuration": 0.05,
    "timeStep": 5e-7,
    "solverType": "gear-shichman"
  }'

Request Model (optional fields): 

{
  "simulationDuration": 0.05,
  "timeStep": 5e-7,
  "solverType": "gear-shichman"
}

Response: 200 OK 

{
  "circuitId": "circuit-uuid-001",
  "name": "circuit",
  "componentCount": 24,
  "parameters": {
    "simulationDuration": 0.05,
    "timeStep": 5e-7,
    "solverType": "gear-shichman"
  },
  "components": [...]
}

Valid Solver Types: - backward-euler - Implicit 1st order (stable, for stiff circuits) - trapezoidal - Implicit 2nd order (balanced accuracy/stability) - gear-shichman - Variable order (best for variable dynamics)

docs.text:

  • Parameter update only affects simulation settings, not component parameters (use clone for component changes)
  • Batch cancellation is asynchronous; may take 1-2 seconds to complete

docs.title: Architecture Improvements
docs.text:
New Classes in gecko-rest-api:

  • gecko.rest.api.dto.BatchJobStatus - Aggregated batch progress and per-simulation status
  • gecko.rest.api.dto.CircuitCloneRequest - Clone request with optional parameter overrides
  • gecko.rest.api.controller.BatchSimulationController - GET/DELETE batch endpoints
  • gecko.rest.api.controller.CircuitManagementController - Clone and parameter update endpoints

REST API Endpoints Added:

  • GET /api/v1/simulations/batch/{batchId} - Batch status and progress
  • DELETE /api/v1/simulations/batch/{batchId} - Cancel batch

docs.text:

docs.text:

  • Batch cancellation requires valid batch ID (no wildcard/regex matching)
